title: Old-time parades: costumes, lights, social clubs and wagon advertising
summary: Arthur describes tuxedo-clad marshals, night parades with battery lights, rival clubs, and bands on wagons advertising balls.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Right. It's too big. Anything about the style of the music that's any much different or the way the parades are organized or going, anything different much in the old days if you can remember?

I don't know. I think the old days the parade was, to my eye just from what I've seen, I think they were nicer than they have now. Because the parades were, they dressed in tuxedo suits with the big pigeons on their shoulders and the big stream was down the front, you know.

And they had the grand marshall and they had, they called the aides on the side, they'd have maybe the grand marshall, they'd have maybe six, eight or twelve aides on the side. And they would dress something like the grand marshall, but he'd have a longer. A little fancier. A little fancier thing, I mean they had that. And they wore those, they wore those big pigeons on their shoulders, stuffed pigeons, and those high beaver hats. They don't have that in the parades now. The fellas just wear silk shirts and an umbrella and they go along dancing. It's way different from in the times when I seen parades when I was a kid, when my dad and them were playing. And they didn't have as much, the fellas do a lot of dancing and shaking in the parade. But in them days those guys just stepped proud, man. They were proud steppers, those fellas that were in the parades in them times, you know. And then they would have, they would have carriages with the horses hooked in them. And the carriages would be all decorated and they'd have batteries in them. They'd have lights all around the carriages. And oh it was pretty. And even the fellas that were in the parade would have batteries in their pockets and they'd light the pigeon up, you know, press the battery and the pigeon would light up. It was real nice in them times. Much nicer than now, the parades were anyhow. And the bands were large.
I imagine they would be better in those days. Yeah.
And then they used to, they didn't parade in the day.
They'd have night parades then. They used to parade at night.

That's why I used to have parade at night, because they had all those lights on them and those batteries and everything. And all those horses would be all decorated up with those little lights on them, battery lights. The fellas sitting in the carriage riding, they'd just press their buttons and the horses would light up, you know. All the harness and everything would light up pretty. And they'd leave it go for a certain amount of time. Then they'd put it out and maybe the next carriage he'd light up. It was real nice doing them parades they had. And then time they had the Art Fellas, they had the Bulls Club. You heard of the Bulls Club? Oh yeah. The Art Fellas, the Bulls Club, they had the Santa Sinners, and they had the Lions Club. Those were the clubs that used to parade. They used to try and outdo one another. That's what made the parade so nice. Each club would try and have a nicer parade than the other fella. Yeah. I remember those things. Well, then I'd been growing up to be a boy around about 15 or 16 year old, and them times I remember that well. But I thought the parades and them days was much nicer than that. And then we had more. Then they used to have, like say when they had a ball at a hall and it did, they would have, they'd advertise the same day of the ball. They wouldn't do like they do now, have those bills printed and put them on posts. They didn't do like that. What they did that Sunday morning, they'd get a band and they'd put it on a moving wagon, and them days they had moving wagons, a big long moving wagon with the horses. You remember those bands? Well then they'd get a band, the band that was going to play that night would get in that wagon that Sunday morning, and then they would parade all around the street in the neighborhoods to draw the people, and they would play music at each corner they'd go to, they'd play a piece. Then they'd go to the next corner and they'd play a piece. Then they'd just go all over down there, and then all in the trimmie, that's how they would advertise the dancing MVs. Of course they could afford that band at them times because those fellas didn't get but about a dollar and a half a night to play music a piece. That is the musicians, and on the truck they'd get a dollar a day to play on that truck. They would play until about, say from about nine o'clock the morning until about eleven o'clock, you see, eleven, twelve o'clock they would stop. Then they'd rest up for that night. And we'd sit in that band on the wagon, and playing at the hall that night, those fellas wouldn't even make four and a half. That's right, you could hire a band in them days for fifteen dollars. Fifteen dollars for a band. You'd give them a deposit, like say if there was going to be seven pieces, you'd give them, uh, well I guess about, let's see, seven pieces, about three and a half. Each man you'd get a sense of deposit, on the job that night.
